# Ezekiel 43: Research Notes

## Background: how the whole vision (chs. 40–48) is read

This question shapes almost every verse, so it comes first.

- **Dispensational (literal future millennium).** On this view the temple will be built during Christ's thousand-year reign. Its sacrifices can't forgive sins, because Christ has already done that once for all; they're seen as memorials or ceremonial cleansings. https://www.gotquestions.org/Ezekiel-temple.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel/charismatic) holds this view but stresses that the text never says "build." If the temple is built, God will do it, not people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/
  - Chuck Smith says these chapters concern Israel in the "Kingdom Age," not the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/c2000_Eze/Eze_040.cfm
  - Preceptaustin cites LaHaye and Ice, who list "animal sacrifices offered as memorials to Christ's death." It argues that reading the text literally and consistently leads to a millennial temple. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_millennium_3
- **Reformed (symbolic, fulfilled in Christ).**
  - Ligonier argues the temple was never meant to be built. Its measurements look symbolic (a perfect square, multiples of five), and the returned exiles were never blamed for failing to build it. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-sees-new-temple
  - Kim Riddlebarger (amillennial) says Ezekiel pictures the new earth in the temple language his readers knew, and that Revelation 21–22 shows the vision fully realised. https://www.monergism.com/amillennial-interpretation-ezekiel-40-48
- **A middle view (TGC, D. A. Carson).** Carson says the chapters describe the messianic future "in the symbolic categories of Ezekiel's present." He notes that John's city in Revelation has no temple, so Revelation reshapes Ezekiel rather than fulfilling it point for point. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/1-kings-12-philippians-3-ezekiel-42-psalm-94/
- **Desiring God (Baptist site).** Sacrifice stays central, but its focus moves to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice. The new Jerusalem goes beyond Ezekiel's vision. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-temple-did-ezekiel-see
- **History of interpretation.** Guzik quotes a source saying the symbolic church reading was "favored by the church Fathers and the Reformers." He also says Adam Clarke took the temple as the plan the returning exiles were expected to build. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-40.cfm
- **Other readings.**
  - Gill: the worship described is Christian ("evangelical") but written in Old Testament language. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-43.html
  - Pett: an already-existing heavenly temple, with no instruction to build it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html
- **Modern scholarship (a TGC *Themelios* review of Stephen Cook's commentary).** Chapters 38–48 are treated as early ("proto-") apocalyptic writing plus an ideal-world vision written for the exiles. The reviewer notes Ezekiel places the temple well north of Jerusalem. He agrees with Cook that Ezekiel cares more about ordering sacred space than about buildings. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/ezekiel-38-48-a-new-translation-with-introduction-and-commentary/

---

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- After the survey of the temple area, the guide brings Ezekiel back to the outer court's east gate. It was the main entrance, but mainly it was the way the coming vision of God would pass. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/43-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Wesley: the glory left eastward and now returns from the east. Here God's "voice" is real speech, not thunder. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-43.html
- Guzik: the glory comes back the way it left. God fills readily and withdraws only reluctantly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/
- Matthew Henry: this is the glory of Israel's covenant God. Idols have only the glory their craftsmen give them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_043.cfm
- Benson:
  - "Behold" expresses joy and wonder.
  - The return signals that God again accepts the place.
  - "Many waters" stands either for the terror of God's judgments or the power of His word.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/43-1.htm
- Utley (bible.org): the returning presence shows the ancient covenant has been restored. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-43
- Chuck Smith links the "many waters" voice to Revelation 1 and takes it as Christ's return in glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-13.html
- Gotquestions says some see this entry as the triumphal entry (Matthew 21). It also notes the popular link to the walled-up Eastern Gate, which it points out is not the gate Jesus used. https://www.gotquestions.org/eastern-gate-Jerusalem.html

**v. 3**
- "When He came to destroy the city" means when Ezekiel *announced* its destruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-43.html
- A commentary on Biblehub quotes Hitzig: the prophet "destroyed" the city in idea by prophesying it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/43-1.htm
- Matthew Henry: God appears the same way because He doesn't change. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_043.cfm
- Pulpit homily: Ezekiel saw no difference between the glory of judgment and the glory of mercy. God is the same in both. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- Pett links the vision to ch. 1 and chs. 8–10. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html

**v. 4**
- Wesley: Israel's sins drove the glory out, and their repentance brings it back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-43.html
- Ligonier compares this to the glory cloud filling Solomon's temple as a sign of God's approval. For the exiles it was a resounding "no" to the fear that God had left for good. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-returns-his-temple
- Pett: God returns to His own temple, not a man-made one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the finished structure needed God's acceptance through His glory, as with the Tabernacle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm
- Pulpit homily: the glory filling the house pictures God's presence spreading through the whole church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html

**v. 6**
- **Who is speaking?**
  - Most interpreters say Jehovah Himself. Hengstenberg and Schröder say "the man" (as the angel of the Lord). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
  - Ellicott says God, and thinks "the man" is probably the same guide as before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm
  - The Biblehub commentary page records further debate (Hävernick, Kliefoth, Hitzig). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/43-1.htm
- **Who is "the man"?**
  - Wesley: "The man" is Christ, standing by to strengthen Ezekiel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-43.html
  - Matthew Henry: we couldn't bear God's voice unless Christ stood by us as Mediator. If the man was a created angel, he stood by as a fellow learner. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_043.cfm

**v. 7**
- Wesley:
  - "Throne": God rules as king in grace.
  - "Feet": God's resting place, in the temple as the type and in the church as the fulfilment.
  - Kings may have been buried in idol temples.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/ezekiel-43.html
- Ellicott:
  - "Forever" is what sets this temple apart. The Tabernacle, Solomon's temple and the rebuilt temple all passed away.
  - "Shall not defile" is a plain future statement, not a command, which fits the ideal character of the vision.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): the temple was a type of Christ's incarnation (John 2:19–21). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-43.html
- Guzik (dispensational): the "forever" promise goes further than any promise about the Tabernacle or Solomon's temple. It shows God isn't finished with Israel or its land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/
- Utley: this reflects the new covenant of 36:22–36, where a new heart makes obedience possible. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-43
- **"Prostitution."** Commentators agree it means idolatry. One textual reading has "in their high places," another "at their deaths." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- **"Corpses/funeral offerings of their kings."**
  - Rosenmüller and Hävernick: dead idols. Ewald, Hitzig and Kliefoth: literal royal graves near the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/43-1.htm
  - Guzik quotes three options: kings buried too near the temple, human sacrifice to Molech, or idols called "carcasses." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/

**v. 8**
- Gill: the "wall" is either sin separating Israel from God or the bare wall standing between their altars and His. He links this to Manasseh's altars (2 Kings 21:4). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-43.html
- Biblehub's study page also points to Manasseh's defilement of the temple. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/43.htm
- Pett's application: don't presume on God as Solomon did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html
- Preceptaustin's bracketed comment applies "consumed them in My anger" to the Great Tribulation, a distinctly dispensational reading. https://www.preceptaustin.org/the_millennium_3

**v. 9**
- Clarke: David and most kings of Judah were buried on Zion near the temple. God wants the area kept pure. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-43.html
- **Is the promise conditional?**
  - Coffman: God's dwelling "forever" depends completely on Israel's holiness (vv. 9–12). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-13.html
  - Utley: the conditions in vv. 9 and 11 test obedience. Israel failed every earlier temple and can obey only after the new covenant. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-43
  - Contrast Ellicott, who treats v. 7 as a sure promise (above).

**v. 10**
- Matthew Henry: undeserved mercy should bring a repentant shame. God's goodness leads to repentance. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_043.cfm
- Pulpit homily: love achieves what the law couldn't. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- Clarke: let them measure themselves against the pattern they should have lived by. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-43.html
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: departing from the Mosaic pattern went with sin, so restoring the pattern stood for returning to obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-43.html
- Guzik: the message is that God isn't finished with them, told as real things that would happen, not "fairy tales." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the conditional "if" shows that the people's holiness and God's dwelling go together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm
- Clarke: "if" means true repentance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-43.html
- Matthew Henry: along with God's promised blessings we must learn our duties. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_043.cfm
- Pett: the Hebrew word for "form/design" appears only here, four times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html

**v. 12**
- Pulpit (citing Smend): "This is the law" is the standard heading formula of the priestly law codes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- Guzik: holiness is the founding principle of the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/
- Biblehub's study page: no casual approach to God, with 1 Peter 1:16 as the New Testament echo. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/43.htm
- Pett: Israel later turned these laws into an end in themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html
- Ligonier: holiness spreads beyond Jerusalem until all creation is God's temple. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/new-most-holy-place

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: a new section starts here and runs to ch. 46. It fittingly opens with the altar, the centre of worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm
- Clarke: this is the same cubit used before, a handbreadth (about 4 inches) longer than the Babylonian cubit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/ezekiel/43.htm
- Gill: the altar is a type of Christ (Hebrews 13:10). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-43.html
- Guzik: like every true altar, it points to the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-43/
- Desiring God calls the altar the "architectural center" of the temple. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-temple-did-ezekiel-see

**v. 14**
- Clarke: this altar is bigger than the one in Exodus 27, which had to be portable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/ezekiel/43.htm

**v. 15**
- Clarke explains two Hebrew words:
  - *harel*: "mount of God."
  - *ariel*: "lion of God," perhaps the hearth, because it devours offerings the way a lion devours prey.
  - https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-43.html
- Gill links "ariel" to Christ, the Lion of Judah, but prefers "fire of God." He sees the horns as Christ's strength to save. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-15.html
- Constable: the horns stand for strength. Barnes notes victims may have been tied to the horns (Psalm 118:27). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-15.html

**vv. 16–17**
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary quotes the Speaker's Commentary on the numbers: 12 for the tribes, 4 for the earth, 14 as twice 7 (the covenant number). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-43.html
- Pett: Exodus 20 had forbidden steps up to an altar, but they were needed here. The stepped shape suggests reaching heavenward. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: only the altar needs cleansing because Jehovah is already in the house. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- Gill: "ordinances" refers to the sacrifices that follow, not the measurements. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-18.html
- **A key point of disagreement.** Gotquestions treats 43:18–46:24 as the fullest passage on sacrifices in the millennium. It says they are object lessons about sin, not means of forgiveness (Hebrews 10:4). https://www.gotquestions.org/millennial-sacrifices.html

**v. 19**
- Pulpit: Ezekiel acts as God's prophet, but unlike Moses he works through the priests (note the "they" in vv. 22–26). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- Constable: Zadok's line was the honoured priestly line (1 Kings 2:35). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-20.html
- Pett argues against the millennial view here: a privilege for Zadok's sons only makes sense right after the exile, since they were as guilty as anyone of Christ's crucifixion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-43.html
- Biblehub's study page: these sacrifices point to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/43.htm

**v. 20**
- Gill: putting on the blood pictures the gospel ministry of holding out Christ's blood and its blessings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-20.html
- Ellicott: some steps of the Mosaic ritual (pouring out the rest of the blood, burning the fat) go unmentioned because Ezekiel assumes readers know them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm

**v. 21**
- Ellicott quotes this verse but adds no comment of his own on it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: "finished the purification" means that day's sin offering. Verse 25 shows both sin and burnt offerings were made on each of the seven days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/43.htm

**v. 24**
- The burnt offering was the perfect sacrifice because it was wholly consumed and given to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-43.html

**vv. 25–26**
- Clarke: Ezekiel spells out the details as if the book of the law had been lost, so the exiles could follow them back in the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/ezekiel/43.htm

**v. 27**
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: true worship is sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-43.html
- Pulpit homily: being accepted rests on a substitute's death. The animal sacrifices taught that only God's Son's perfect sacrifice could actually work. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-43.html
- A comment on the Studylight page calls this a "mystical" altar, since "Christ is our altar." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/43-20.html
- Gotquestions (dispensational) suggests the sacrifices may serve national cleansing for Israel, or be memorials. https://www.gotquestions.org/the-LORD-is-there.html
- TGC: once the glory returns, the restoration is complete. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ezekiel/

---

## Where Protestant traditions clearly differ (summary)
1. **Is the temple future and literal?**
   - Yes: the dispensational/charismatic teachers (Guzik, Chuck Smith, Gotquestions, Preceptaustin).
   - No, it's symbolic or fulfilled in Christ and the new creation: the Reformed teachers (Ligonier, Riddlebarger).
   - Something in between: TGC (Carson) and Desiring God.
2. **What do the sacrifices in vv. 18–27 mean?** Memorials or object lessons in a future millennium (dispensational), or types pointing to Christ the altar (Gill, Clarke, Pulpit).
3. **Is the "forever" of vv. 7–9 conditional?** Coffman and Utley stress the condition; Ellicott treats it as a sure promise.
4. **Who are "the man" and the speaker in v. 6?** Wesley (Methodist) and Matthew Henry say Christ the Mediator; others say an angel or the guide.

## What I couldn't find
I found nothing in these areas, so the notes leave them out:
- Catholic or Orthodox sources (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org).
- Lutheran sources (LCMS, 1517).
- NET Bible translators' notes or Bible Odyssey.
- Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

The Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran gaps are because the searches ran out, not because nothing exists. Good next pages to read in full are the Enduring Word, Gill and Wesley chapter pages above; I could only see extracts of them.
